But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched every day in the modeled dataset. The dispatch strategy is modified for shoulder- season days where heating or cooling load is assumed to be minimal, defined by an average daily temperature greater than 50°F and less than 68°F. On those days, load shifting (done via precooling or preheating) is not dispatched, but load-shedding events are dispatched. The method for choosing this temperature range is described in section 4.2 Initial Sensitivity Analysis. Because of the unrealistically high number of days that demand flexibility is dispatched in this upgrade, the results must be used thoughtfully. One approach is to use daily profiles from the baseline for most days of the year and to splice in daily profiles from the upgrade for days when the intent of the analysis is to dispatch demand flexibility. Similarly, annualized energy consumption or energy savings metrics should not be used because of the overrepresentation of dispatch. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 ResStock Baseline Approach The baseline assumption for thermostats in ResStock is a range of heating and cooling set points and setbacks or setups derived from the Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, which vary based on climate zone, building type, HVAC type, and tenure (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023). These set points are assumed to apply year-round. Approximately one-third of dwelling units are assumed to have heating and/or cooling thermostat setbacks or setups, where the set point is changed by the homeowner during part of each day. The distribution of set points in the building stock is shown in Figure 1. ResStock makes no explicit assumption about whether these setbacks or setups are achieved using manual adjustment, a programmable thermostat, or a smart thermostat. In practice, demand response programs typically incentivize or directly pay for customers to install smart thermostats as a condition of program participation. Figure 1.
